lesson.title: Goods and Services: What's the Difference?
lesson.subject: social-studies

contentBlocks.text: Yesterday you sorted needs and wants. Today let's learn two more important words: goods and services — the two ways people meet those needs and wants.

A good is a real, physical thing you can hold or touch — like bread, a bicycle, or a book. A service is help or work that someone does for you — like a haircut, a doctor's checkup, or a teacher teaching a lesson. Think about your day: what goods did you use? What services did someone provide for you?
Every day, you use goods and receive services from people all around your community. Tomorrow we'll look at how a whole community works together to meet everyone's needs.

objectives: Define a good as a physical, tangible item and a service as work or help someone provides
Correctly sort real examples into goods and services
teacherGuide.facilitationScript:
1. Ask the child to name something they touched today (a good) and something someone did to help them (a service).
2. Introduce the definitions clearly with those real examples.
3. Sort 4-5 more examples together (bread, a haircut, a book, a doctor visit).
4. Move to the worksheet: sort each item into goods or services.
5. Close by asking the child to think of one goods-provider and one service-provider in their own community.
differentiationTips: Struggling: use only very clear-cut examples (a toy vs. a haircut) before tackling trickier ones
Ready for more: discuss a business that provides both — a restaurant sells food (a good) and provides serving (a service)
For a child who enjoys community helpers, connect back to last year's helper jobs and sort each as providing a good or a service
teacherGuide.answerKey: 1. Bread = good. 2. Haircut = service. 3. Bicycle = good. 4. Doctor's checkup = service. 5. Teaching a lesson = service.
teacherGuide.standardsRationale: Distinguishing goods from services is a core Grade 2 economics concept (matching the C3 Framework's economics dimension), directly building on yesterday's needs-vs-wants foundation.

generationData.instructions: Sort each item as a GOOD (a physical thing) or a SERVICE (help or work someone does).
